output.title: Elevated ble_disconnects_24h rate on firmware 1.4.2
output.summary: Devices on firmware 1.4.2 show a roughly 6.8x higher ble_disconnects_24h rate than 1.4.1 in the current window (10.53 vs 1.54 disconnects/device-day), with the rate-ratio CI excluding one, matching the triage candidate. This holds even when app version is held fixed at 3.2 for both firmware groups, so the effect is not explained by the app-version confound that initially looked plausible given 100% of 1.4.2 devices also run app 3.2. Release notes show 1.4.2 shortened the BLE supervision timeout from 4s to 2s and moved retry backoff to a tighter exponential cap, intended for faster drop detection — a change that mechanically increases counted disconnect events. Session_gap_minutes, a proxy for user-facing connectivity loss, shows no significant difference between 1.4.1 and 1.4.2 (ratio near 1, CI not excluding one), and zero support tickets tagged connectivity/battery/app-sync matched in the current window. This pattern is consistent with either (a) a genuine increase in connection instability on 1.4.2, or (b) a measurement-definition shift where the same underlying radio behavior is now logged as more, shorter disconnects without a corresponding increase in user-visible session gaps. A structurally similar historical incident (1.3.0 disconnect cluster) was initially attributed to a firmware radio change and later found to be a phone-OS-side issue, so a firmware-first read here should be held cautiously pending further characterization.

leading_hypothesis.statement: Firmware 1.4.2's revised BLE connection-supervisor timing (4s->2s supervision timeout, shorter exponential retry backoff) is associated with a large increase in counted ble_disconnects_24h events relative to 1.4.1, an association that persists after controlling for app version.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: App 3.2's rewritten background-sync scheduler, not the firmware change, drives the higher disconnect count, since all 1.4.2 devices in this window also run app 3.2.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Compare ble_disconnects_24h between 1.4.1 and 1.4.2 while holding app_version at 3.2 for both groups; this was already done (rate 1.54 vs 10.53), and the gap persisted, weakening but not fully eliminating a residual app interaction.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: The 1.4.2 change to a 2s supervision timeout is a measurement/definition shift that logs more, shorter disconnect events without a corresponding increase in user-visible session interruption.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: If session_gap_minutes and reconnection-latency telemetry remain unchanged between 1.4.1 and 1.4.2 while support tickets stay flat, that would support the artifact explanation; a rise in either would argue against it. Current session_gap_minutes comparison shows no significant difference, but outdoor/body-block/commuting RF conditions were not re-characterized in the soak lab per release notes, leaving this open.

ble_disconnects_24h, app version held at 3.2: 1.4.2 rate

ble_disconnects_24h rate by region, benelux (1.4.2, current window)
ble_disconnects_24h rate by region, dach (1.4.2, current window)

supporting_evidence.claim: The 1.4.1-vs-1.4.2 disconnect rate ratio's confidence interval excludes one, matching the triage candidate's ci_excludes_one flag.
The elevated disconnect rate on 1.4.2 persists when app version is held constant at 3.2, weakening a pure app-confound explanation.
The disconnect rate elevation is broadly uniform across regions (roughly 10.0-10.8 disconnects/device-day), consistent with a firmware-wide rather than regional-RF-specific effect.

Firmware 1.4.2 release notes document a supervision-timeout reduction from 4s to 2s and a tighter exponential retry backoff, explicitly intended for faster drop detection, which provides a documented mechanism that could increase counted disconnect events.

counter_evidence.claim: session_gap_minutes, a proxy for user-facing connectivity interruption, shows no significant difference between 1.4.1 and 1.4.2 (ratio near 1, confidence interval not excluding one).
No support tickets tagged connectivity, battery, or app-sync matched in the current window for firmware 1.4.2, despite the large telemetry-side increase.

1.4.2's own release notes state that soak-lab testing (indoor office RF) showed link-loss counts in the same band as 1.4.1, and that outdoor, body-block, and commuting RF were not re-characterized for this train, so field conditions rather than the firmware change itself may explain the field-observed rise.

A structurally similar historical firmware disconnect cluster (1.3.0) was initially attributed to the firmware's interval change but was later found to be caused by a phone OS Bluetooth stack on a beta channel, illustrating that a firmware radio note co-occurring with a disconnect rise is not proof of firmware causation.

recommended_actions.description: Re-characterize 1.4.2 BLE link-loss behavior in outdoor, body-block, and commuting RF conditions (not covered by the original indoor soak lab) to determine whether the field disconnect rise reflects real conditions the lab did not test.

Obtain or instrument per-event disconnect duration/reconnection-latency data to test whether the 2s-vs-4s supervision timeout change is primarily reclassifying brief link hiccups as full disconnects, versus producing genuinely longer or more frequent connection loss.

Monitor support ticket volume for connectivity/battery tags on 1.4.2 devices over the next reporting window before deciding on any firmware rollback or hotfix, since current ticket volume is flat despite the telemetry signal.

uncertainty: Whether the 1.4.2 supervision-timeout change causes genuinely more connection instability or merely counts pre-existing brief radio drops as distinct disconnect events is not resolved by the available metrics.
No phone-OS or device-model breakdown is available to rule out a phone-side contribution analogous to the prior 1.3.0 incident.
Support-ticket volume is a lagging and possibly low-sensitivity indicator for this kind of background radio metric, so its current absence does not conclusively rule out user impact.
Cohort size in this window (100 devices on 1.4.2) is a beta-scale population; broader-fleet behavior at general availability is unverified.

arguments.description: Firmware update causing increased BLE disconnects per device day

arguments.query: firmware 1.4.2 BLE radio interval change disconnect
1.4.2 firmware release notes connection supervisor retry backoff changes

output.title: Skin-irritation / adhesion tag cluster — flat-trend check against known high-motion adhesive characterization
output.summary: The skin-irritation tag cluster (22 affected users, flat trend, CI does not exclude one) shows adhesion_flag and skin_temp_delta_c telemetry essentially unchanged between prior and current windows, and no firmware version shows a statistically distinguishable adhesion rate from another. Feedback text sampled under this tag matches the pattern already documented internally as an open, unresolved adhesive-design characterization (high motion intensity plus elevated patch-site temperature delta), not a new firmware- or lot-specific defect. Because the internal playbook explicitly forbids treating this pattern as closed/benign even when it looks like baseline characterization, and because affected-user counts and prior-event counts show some increase, the signal cannot be confidently dismissed as noise nor confirmed as a new incident.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The current skin-irritation/adhesion tickets are associated with the pre-existing, unresolved high-motion adhesive-lift characterization (elevated motion intensity with elevated skin-temp delta) rather than with any single firmware version, app version, or hardware lot.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A specific firmware version (e.g., 1.2.0, which showed the highest point-rate) is driving the adhesion/skin-irritation tickets.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: compare_versions on adhesion_flag between 1.2.0 and 1.4.2 showed a rate ratio whose confidence interval includes one, so this was tested and not supported by current data.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A new hardware adhesive lot defect (similar to the historical INC-2025-031 confirmed lot recall) is responsible for this cluster.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Pull lot/batch identifiers for the affected devices in the sampled feedback and check for concentration in a single lot; if a lot split shows disproportionate representation, escalate as a possible hardware incident per KD-03/KD-06 guidance.

deterministic_findings.label: adhesion_flag rate ratio, firmware 1.2.0 vs 1.4.2 (current window)
feedback records matching skin irritation query, current window

supporting_evidence.claim: Adhesion_flag telemetry rate is essentially flat between prior and current windows (0.125 to 0.136 flags per device-day), consistent with the triage-reported flat trend.
Skin-temp delta telemetry did not rise between windows; it was slightly lower in the current window, which does not support a worsening thermal driver.

Sampled feedback tagged skin-irritation/adhesion/comfort-fit describes adhesive lift during high-intensity sessions with a hot/red mark at the patch site, spread across firmware 1.2.0, 1.4.0, and 1.4.2 and across multiple regions, not concentrated in one version.

A rate-ratio comparison of adhesion_flag between the highest-rate firmware (1.2.0) and a low-rate firmware (1.4.2) had a confidence interval spanning one, indicating no statistically distinguishable firmware effect in this window.

Internal known-issues documentation describes lift rates rising when motion intensity and skin-temp delta are jointly elevated, and states this remains an open, unresolved adhesive-design item that must not be waved away as expected.

Support playbook guidance states adhesion/skin-irritation clusters are not closed known issues and must be logged and escalated to operations rather than dismissed as characteristic, even though a prior lot recall (INC-2025-031) was a genuine confirmed hardware incident.

counter_evidence.claim: A tag-restricted feedback search for the exact current and prior windows returned zero matched records under the skin-irritation tag filter, only surfacing results once the tag filter was removed and a broader text query was used, suggesting some fragility in how this cluster is indexed/labeled.
Neither adhesion_flag nor skin_temp_delta_c telemetry shows a meaningful upward shift between prior and current windows, which weighs against an acute new escalation.

recommended_actions.description: Log this cluster against the existing open adhesive-design item (KI-AD-007) rather than closing it as characteristic, per support playbook guidance.

Pull lot/batch identifiers for the devices in the sampled skin-irritation/adhesion tickets and check for concentration in a single hardware lot, to rule in or out a lot-specific defect similar to the historical confirmed recall.
Continue trend monitoring of adhesion_flag and skin_temp_delta_c telemetry over the next reporting window before deciding whether this remains within known baseline characterization.

uncertainty: Feedback search behavior differed sharply between tag-filtered (zero matches) and unfiltered text queries (26 matches) for the same windows, raising a question about tag-indexing completeness that was not fully resolved.
No lot/batch-level breakdown tool was available to directly test the lot-defect alternative hypothesis; this remains open.
Triage-reported affected_users (22) and prior_events (13) could not be independently cross-checked against a per-device tool in this investigation; they are taken as given triage quantities.

arguments.description: Skin irritation and adhesion complaints clustering, low affected user count, flat trend, checking for lot defect or firmware correlation

output.title: Rising claims-interpretation ticket cluster — readiness score misread as clinical result
output.summary: Support/feedback tickets tagged claims-interpretation rose from 2 in the prior window to 21 in the current window, with wearers repeatedly describing the readiness score as if it were a medical/clinical result ('health verdict', 'lab result', 'clinical finding'). The cluster spans multiple firmware versions (1.2.0 through 1.4.2), multiple app versions (3.0, 3.1, 3.2), and multiple regions, with no concentration on a single firmware or app build. This pattern matches a previously closed communications incident (INC-2025-002) in which on-screen copy — not hardware or scoring-code defects — drove a similar misread cluster, closed as a comms/claims risk under policy KD-05. The current cluster is best read as a recurrence of that same claims-shaped, copy-driven pattern rather than a new device defect.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The rise in claims-interpretation tickets is associated with wearers reading the on-screen readiness score/copy as a clinical or diagnostic result, in a pattern consistent across firmware and app versions rather than tied to any specific build, mirroring the copy-driven mechanism documented in the closed comms incident INC-2025-002.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A firmware- or app-version-specific defect (e.g., altered score calculation or a broken UI label on one build) is producing scores or copy that look clinical to users.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: compare_versions on adhesion/motion/skin-temp or a UI-related metric across the firmware versions present in the sample (1.2.0, 1.3.0, 1.4.0, 1.4.1, 1.4.2) and app versions (3.0, 3.2); ticket counts already show representation across all of them rather than isolation to one build, which weakens a single-build defect story.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: The increase is driven by a single high-volume region or channel amplifying a local translation/localization issue.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: run search_feedback with tag claims-interpretation broken down by region to check whether tickets concentrate in one region/locale versus being spread across uk, nordics, dach, benelux, iberia as seen in the current sample.

supporting_evidence.claim: Current-window claims-interpretation tickets co-occur heavily with data-accuracy tags (18 of 21) and repeat near-identical phrasing about the score being mistaken for a health verdict or clinical finding.
The cluster is spread across firmware versions 1.2.0, 1.3.0, 1.4.0, 1.4.1, and 1.4.2 and app versions 3.0 and 3.2 in the sampled records, not concentrated on one build.

A prior closed incident, INC-2025-002, involved readiness screenshots being treated as clinical results and was closed as a communications incident, not a hardware or scoring-code incident, with policy KD-05 issued as the fix.

Product policy states the readiness score must not be placed adjacent to clinical vocabulary in UI chrome, and that claims-misread tickets should be routed to a dedicated queue rather than treated as a clinical or hardware incident.

counter_evidence.claim: Some current-window tickets in the same tag show users self-correcting after reading help content ('Read the help article — score is not a medical result'), suggesting the underlying copy/education path can resolve confusion for at least some users.

knowledge_sources.title: Historical Incident Log — Kestrel Loop
knowledge_sources.section: INC-2025-002 — Readiness screenshots as clinical results (comms)

recommended_actions.description: Route this ticket cluster to the claims-misread queue (KD-03) and file a Communications copy-review request citing KD-05, since the pattern spans firmware and app versions and matches the prior copy-driven comms incident rather than a device defect.

Audit current on-screen placement of the readiness score relative to clinical-sounding vocabulary (e.g., wording near 'ready'/score display) across app versions 3.0 through 3.2 to identify a specific copy element driving the misread.
Run a regional breakdown of claims-interpretation tickets to rule out a localization/translation-specific driver before closing this as a pure copy-placement issue.

uncertainty: The exact on-screen copy or UI element causing the misread has not been directly inspected in this investigation; the conclusion rests on ticket text similarity and precedent, not a UI audit.
Regional concentration was not fully broken down; a locale-specific translation driver has not been ruled out.
Whether the current cluster will resolve on its own (as some current-window tickets show self-correction via help content) or requires a copy change is not yet determined.

arguments.description: Users misinterpreting wellness readiness score as a medical/clinical diagnosis, rising support tickets tagged claims-interpretation

arguments.query: INC-2025-002 prior comms event readiness score copy

output.title: Overheating tag cluster traced to known Nordics cold-weather battery drain characteristic
output.summary: The overheating-tagged feedback cluster (26 current, 25 prior records, essentially flat) co-occurs almost entirely with battery and app-ui tags and describes phones/devices feeling 'warm' during cold-weather use or while syncing, not a thermal safety event. Device-level skin_temp_delta_c telemetry shows no regional or window-over-window elevation (all regions ~1.31-1.36 C/device-day, current vs prior essentially flat). In contrast, battery_drain_pct is markedly elevated in Nordics (17.3%) versus other regions (12.8-13.0%), matching a documented standing, benign known issue (KI-NW-014) present since firmware 1.2.0 and unrelated to the current 1.4.x trains. The 'overheating' language in tickets appears to originate from the app's low-battery/sync warning screens being perceived as alarming, not from elevated device temperature.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The overheating tag cluster is a mislabeling of the pre-existing Nordics cold-weather battery drain characteristic (KI-NW-014): users see steep battery drop and alarming sync/battery UI screens in cold conditions and describe the phone or device as feeling warm, while objective skin_temp_delta_c telemetry shows no elevation in Nordics or any other region.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A genuine thermal event on the device (e.g., charging or motion-driven heat) is causing the overheating reports.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Check skin_temp_delta_c broken down by firmware/app version and cohort for any subgroup elevated above the ~1.3-1.4 C/device-day baseline; none found in the region breakdown examined.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A firmware regression in a recent train (e.g., 1.4.2) introduced new overheating behavior.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: KD-04 states the Nordics drain characteristic is present from 1.2.0 through current 1.4.x and was not introduced by 1.4.2; sample tickets span firmware 1.2.0 through 1.4.2 with no version concentration.

supporting_evidence.claim: All five sampled current-window overheating tickets also carry the battery and app-ui tags and describe cold-weather battery drain or warmth during syncing, not spontaneous device heat.
Prior-window sampled tickets show the same pattern of cold-weather drain complaints co-tagged overheating/battery/app-ui.
A historical incident with nearly identical framing (Nordics winter drain tickets) was closed as not-an-incident and encoded as a standing known issue KI-NW-014.

The known issues register documents Nordics battery_drain_pct running ~4.3 percentage points above other regions in both the current and prior 14-day windows, present since firmware 1.2.0 and not introduced by 1.4.2.
Communications policy explicitly instructs that this Nordics drain elevation is a regional engineering characteristic and must not be described as a health or thermal safety event.

counter_evidence.claim: skin_temp_delta_c shows no meaningful regional or window-over-window elevation, so there is no telemetry signal of an actual thermal anomaly underlying the overheating tag.

knowledge_sources.section: KI-NW-014 Nordics elevated daily battery drain (standing, benign)

knowledge_sources.title: Known Issues Register — Kestrel Loop
knowledge_sources.section: What the field export actually shows

recommended_actions.description: Route overheating-tagged tickets that co-occur with battery/app-ui tags to the existing KI-NW-014 known-issue workflow rather than opening a new hardware investigation.
Review the low-battery/sync warning screen copy for wording that could read as a thermal or 'overheating' alert, since support tags appear to be triggered by UI language rather than sensor data.

No user contact or firmware change recommended at this time; continue monitoring skin_temp_delta_c for any future step-change that would distinguish a real thermal event from this known battery characteristic.

uncertainty: Support ticket free text was only sampled (5 of 26 current, 5 of 25 prior records); the full set was not reviewed, so a small number of tickets could still describe genuine thermal discomfort rather than UI/battery confusion.

skin_temp_delta_c was only broken down by region, not by firmware or app version; a version-specific subgroup effect masked in the regional aggregate cannot be fully ruled out within the tool budget used.

The candidate's own affected_users (23) and prior_events (69) figures were provided by triage and were not independently reconciled against the feedback search counts (26 current, 25 prior), which differ somewhat in scope.

arguments.description: Device overheating complaints, skin temperature delta increase, tag overheating
